Protocol for landscape-connectivity-pipelines

Audrey MP

A collection of automated pipelines for landscape connectivity analysis using Graphab, Circuitscape, and related tools.

Github repo for usage license and latest updates here.
Zenodo doi to cite can be found here.

Fast links

  1. GraphabR_paramloop
  2. GraphabR_MAXpathconv
  3. GraphabR_free
  4. Omniscape_loop

Necessary R packages to be installed and loaded:

{library(graph4lg)
library(tidyverse)
library(terra)
library(igraph) 
library(sf)
library(raster) 
library(readr)
library(readxl)}

1. GraphabR_paramloop

Use to run specified combinations of parameters in GraphabR, can take a combination of ‘normal’ runs and ‘metapatch’ runs. Also produces least cost corridors for each combination of runs.

Inputs

Folder should be set up like this, with two folders, a parameter file, the script, .Rproj, and graphab file.

Naming for habitat files Habitat files should be named following this pattern: name_habcodeX_nodataXX where X is a numeric value.

habcode is the value in the raster which is a habitat nodata is the value in the raster which shows no data. The name part of the pattern should be consistent with other files of same species, and for ease of finding. Resistance file naming has no rules, but I like to keep it short and include the sp code for consistency as well.

Set up your parameter table. Set up the combinations of habitat, resistance, minimum area, and interpatch distance (as well as metapatch size and metapatch distance if you are running that) you want to run. Save as params.csv if you are editing from the .xlsx version and put this in the same folder. The script will loop ONLY through the combinations you have put here.

params.csv (can be saved from params.xlsx)
runname Additional prefix that will be added to the name of the files, I usually do sp code. Not important if your habitat files already have a sp code prefix.
hab_file Habitat files path
res_file Resistance files path
minarea Minimum patch size
thr Interpatch distance
metapatch Metapatch size. ONLY FILL IF RUNNING METAPATCH.
metadist Metapatch distance. ONLY FILL IF RUNNING METAPATCH.

Protocol

Outputs

Object Outputs Description
Graphab folders Graphab result folders. Includes the usual output after doing a Graphab run. One folder per combination of parameters set up in the parameters sheet. For metapatch runs, this will be inside another folder.
patches.shp Inside each graphab run. Shows the patches.
ma00_t100-links.shp Links for that combination
ma00_t100-voronoi.shp Components file for that combination
ma00_t100-corridor.shp Least cost corridors
habomni folder Patches files cleaned for omniscape
resomni folder Corridor files cleaned for omniscape
dIIC patches folder Patches file with dIIC values attached
dIIC links folder Links file with dIIC values attached
dIIC nodes folder Nodes file (patch centroids) with dIIC values attached
graphab_results_summary.csv A .csv table showing results of different global landscape metrics for each parameter combination ran (IIC, NC, MSC, SLC).

2. GraphabR_MAXpathconv

Use for obtaining the longest pathways and auto-converting pathways and patches based on conversion scenarios

Inputs

Folder should be set up like this, with four folders, a parameter file and an LULC conversion file, as well as the script, .Rproj, and graphab file.


The most important input is the control sheet (ctl.xlsx). It contains all the parameterisations for the script to run. The order of the sheets inside is important!! The names of the sheets are inconsequential.

ctl.xlsx
Sheet 1: Parameters The default parameters sheet used for running the longest pathways the same with the previous protocol. Change the habitat files, resistance files, and parameters accordingly. If no metapatch value is specified, it automatically runs the normal Graphab (without a metapatch) and vice versa.
Sheet 2: Species Order + Value This table contains the species code and the value you want to change their pathways into during conversion. Important to note that the order of the species (top to bottom) is also the priority order during the combination of the pathways. The first species on the list gets prioritised over the next species and so on.
Sheet 3: Habitat Exclusion for Pathway Conversion This tells the code whether, during the conversion of specific pathways, other species habitats should be excluded. All values above 1 mean exclude that species’ habitat.
Sheet 4, 5 (and possible beyond): Pathway Conversion Scenarios Currently, there are two scenario sheets, but the code will run on any number of scenarios for any sheet that starts with ‘conv); you just need to add more sheets (conv 1, conv2, conv3, etc.). The table shows the scenario in which pathways of each species (column) that overlap certain LULC categories (rows), the values of the pathway will be converted to the amount in the cell.
Sheet 6: Habitat Exclusion for Patch Conversion This tells the code whether, during the conversion of specific pathways, other species habitats should be excluded. All values above 1 mean exclude that species’ habitat. Works the same way as the habitat exclusion for patches but will run for the habitat patches.
Sheet 7, 8 (and possible beyond): Patch Conversion Scenarios Currently, there are two scenario sheets, but the code will run on any number of scenarios for any sheet that starts with ‘pconv’); you just need to add more sheets (pconv1, pconv2, pconv3, etc.). Works the same way as the pathway conversion table.
Other Inputs
habitat folder Folder that includes the .tif files of species habitat rasters, used for running max pathways through Graphab. Remember that the file names here need to be named like: CB_habcode1_nodata9999.tif ![][image11]
resistance folder Folder that includes the .tif files of species resistance rasters, used for running max pathways through Graphab. ![][image12]
convhab folder Folder that includes the .tif files of species habitat, used specifically for habitat exclusion during the conversion step. Put the species code at the start of the file name. ![][image13]
conv.tif .tif file of LULC raster used during the conversion steps. Check that conversion scenario categories match the value in this LULC map. Name should be exactly ‘conv.tif’.
LULC folder Folder that includes the .tif files of LULC for each species, used to add on the final converted pathways of all species.

Protocol

  • Top Pathway Rules: You can change the rules to pick the top pathway in this code line 492-298. For example, to change to top 100: sel <- df$rank <= 100. To change to top 10% quantile: q50 <- quantile(df$dIICCon, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE)

Outputs

Object Outputs Description
overlap.mx.csv .csv file showing overlap between the ‘top’ chosen pathways (from FINpaths) for each species
dIIC_patch folder Patches created from Graphab with dIIC value of the patch.
MAX_ folders Graphab result folders. Includes the usual output after doing a Graphab run. One folder per combination of parameters set up in the parameters sheet.
TOPlinks folder Folder with top pathways only.
FINpaths folder Folder with final paths (buffered, picked for top dIIC) of each species.
FINpathsconv folder Folder with final paths that have gone through the conversion scenario (per species, per conversion scenario).
convLULC folder Final rasters for each species, per conversion scenario, with all added pathways from all species. Ready for pre-processing.
patchconv folder Folder with final patches that have gone through the conversion scenario, ready to be added (per species, per conversion scenario).
FINpathpatch folder Final rasters for each species, per conversion scenario, with all added pathways + patches from all species. Ready for pre-processing.

3. GraphabR_free

With only map rasters as the input and no set parameters, use to select several parameter combinations depending on the landscape inputs and run multiple Graphabs in a loop to produce a broader comparative results space plot

Inputs

The folder should be set up like this, with two folders, a parameter file, the script, .Rproj, and graphab file. File inputs are the same as the GraphabR_paramloop. The main differences are in the params file input, although the same file can be used. If the same file is used, only the habitat and resistance path columns are actually used in this script, the rest are ignored.


An additional R script (‘sumstats.R’) is also included, which is an optional post-loop script to run in addition to the results space plot, some summary statistics. It has potential indices used to normalise the results between landscapes to allow for direct comparisons (this requires further testing).

Difference with GraphabR_paramloop

Main differences

  • It does not require specific parameter combinations to be set beforehand, only input rasters
  • It does not run the graphab_corridor() function to produce least-cost corridors. If corridors are required, the GraphabR_free can be used to first produce the parameters of interest, then have those combinations be run under GraphabR_paramloop
  • It does not save all the Graphab loop outputs to save memory. Only a select number of combinations are saved (this can be changed in the object `selection` line 578-579)

Unlike the base GraphabR_paramloop script, GraphabR_free only requires the habitat and resistance input files and does not require any of the specific parameters (i.e. minimum habitat size, interpatch distance). Instead, these parameters are selected by doing an initial run using a minimum patch size of 1 hectare and selecting all pathways created. The minimum patch size for the initial run can also be changed to <1 ha if testing a map with small patches (<1 ha) or wanting to consider the impact of the map for species with small patch requirements. This change can be done in line 317 (minarea <- n).

From the output of this initial run, we will obtain the distribution of patch sizes as well as pathway lengths. We then use this distribution of values to select ten values of minimum habitat size and interpatch distance to use as parameter combinations for the following Graphab runs. The number of values chosen can be changed in line 523 and line 547 (length.out = n). To note is that the total number of combinations to run will be n2, where n is the number of values selected as parameters.

These figures show an example of how the values are selected. For minimum patch sizes, we select 8 values between the minimum value of 1 ha and a maximum value of the second largest patch size found in the created initial run, equidistant to each other. The second largest rather than the largest patch size was chosen to avoid ‘no pathways created’ if only 1 habitat patch was selected from this method. On the other hand, interpatch distances were selected from values between the first quantile of the distribution of pathway lengths and the maximum pathway length found in the initial run as well, equidistant to each other again. Similarly, the first quantile value was chosen rather than the smallest pathway length to avoid the problem of ‘no pathways created’ if there are no pathways of that length found.

The formula to select the range of values from the distribution of the initial run can be changed both for the patch sizes and the interpatch distance. For example, rather than choosing values equidistant from each other, you can select ten quantiles from the same minimum and maximum values set by the rules above. The formula can be changed in code line 523 (dist_seq for interpatch distance) and line 547 (area_seq for minimum habitat size).


The left-side column shows the distribution of values from an example initial run. The ten values selected from the distribution are shown with the dashed lines. The right-side column shows the relationship between the chosen values, showing that in this instance, the values are chosen equidistant to each other.

Protocol

Outputs

Object Outputs Description
Graphab folders Graphab result folders. Includes the usual output after doing a Graphab run. One folder per combination of parameters set up in the parameters sheet. Only specified parameter combination run results are saved.
graphab_results_summary.csv A .csv table showing results of different global landscape metrics for each parameter combination ran (IIC, NC, MSC, SLC).

Results Space Plot

The results space plot can be plotted from the graphab_results_summary.csv file after the runs are completed. An example code specifically plotting IIC value is at the bottom of the GraphabR_free script, but this code can be adjusted to plot the other global metrics saved in the results .csv such as NC, SLC, MSC.

Allows broad comparisons of the whole landscape across a range of ecological parameters

From the results space, we can see the broad relationship between the changes in both parameters chosen can reflect on the IIC. As the example below, in this environment, there is very little effect of IIC changes from habitat patch size requirements. IIC changes more drastically with interpatch distances, with high interpatch distances producing higher IIC. However, IIC only increases up until an interpatch distance of 10000 where IIC values remain constant afterwards. This shows that in this particular environment, dispersal ability is the main driver of connectivity. Thus, a priority for concern in this area should be short-dispersal species. The results space suggests that species with any habitat requirements show low IIC for short dispersers, suggesting that components are clustered and are disconnected quite far from each other. A potential management plan would be to increase habitat sources in between the main sources of habitats to improve connectivity for short dispersers, whether it be with small or large habitat requirements.


Example results plot space of a landscape. The right plot shows what the resulting Graphab patches and pathway look like.

Testing robustness/sensitivity of chosen parameters

The results plot space can also be used to see how robust the selected parameter combinations are to error. Using the same plot with a red cross as an example for a selected parameter combination (e.g. from expert workshops, literature review) we can see how much error in selecting a value can influence the IIC results. In the example, as minimum habitat size is less sensitive than interpatch distance, even a large error in selecting that parameter does not produce any significant change. On the other hand, depending on how far the actual value of interpatch distance is from the selected value as well as the direction of error, the IIC value could differ significantly. Significant IIC changes occur in the ‘blue bounding box’, specifically in the lower value of interpatch distance. Thus, we can say that in this particular case, the results are robust to any errors of minimum patch size estimate, but are sensitive to interpatch distances >30% different to selected value.


Example results plot space where red X marks an example selected parameter combination. The red box shows IIC for 5% change, purple for 10% change, and blue for 30% change in paramter values.

4. Omniscape_loop

Use to run specified combinations of parameters and input rasters in Omniscape.jl.

For Omniscape requirements, installation, and explanation see here.
For Julia installation see here.

Some personal notes: I found that Omniscape best runs on Julia v1.10 and below. There seems to be a problem when running it with the newest Julia version.

Inputs

Within one folder, with two folders, a parameter .txt file, and the .sh scripts.

inputs.txt (tab-separated)
Resistance file path .tif file
Habitat file path .tif file If using source_from_resistance = TRUE, put “NONE”. If using source_from_resistance = FALSE, put source of habitat file. (“./habitat/…tif).
radius Required.
block size Not required. If no value in the fourth column, then the default block size is 1.

Protocol

Outputs

Object Outputs Description
output folder Each omniscape run will create a folder within the output folder. Name of the folders inside will follow the rule: resfile_habfile_radius
configs folder Collection of the config files created as input for the omniscape run.
logs folder Log text file showing run logs
config Shows full config setting for the omniscape run
cum_currmap Represents total current flowing
flow_potential Represents current flow under ‘null’ resistance
normalized_cum_currmap cum_currmap/flow_potential. Identifies where current is more or less than expected under null.
